title: Sparks Fly in Michigan Senate Debate as El-Sayed and Rogers Trade Fierce Personal and Policy Attacks
snippet: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers clashed over tariffs, Middle East foreign policy, and personal real estate during a tense first debate for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat.
content:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — In a high-stakes showdown that quickly devolved into stinging personal jabs, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers traded heated barbs Thursday evening during their first debate for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat.

The hourlong event, hosted by Grand Rapids NBC affiliate WOOD-TV, highlighted stark ideological contrasts on rising gas prices, foreign conflict in the Middle East, and international tariffs. Yet the debate was equally defined by aggressive insults, prompting veteran moderator Rick Albin to intervene at one point and urge the candidates to rein in their cross-talk.

Tensions Over Tariffs and the Economy

Economic anxiety took center stage early in the broadcast. With ongoing military conflict in Iran driving up costs at the pump, both candidates signaled support for a temporary pause on the federal gas tax. However, they clashed sharply over the root causes of inflation and trade pressure.

El-Sayed, a progressive backed by figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders, accused Rogers of flip-flopping on key foreign and trade issues out of political calculation. Pointing to Canadian trade tariffs implemented under former President Donald Trump that have weighed heavily on Michigan’s border economy, El-Sayed slammed Rogers for changing his tune only after seeing polling numbers drop.

Rogers, a former U.S. Representative and FBI agent, pushed back forcefully, framing El-Sayed as an unrealistic radical selling costly proposals. He targeted El-Sayed’s endorsement of "Medicare for All," warning that progressive spending plans would trigger massive tax hikes and derail private healthcare options. Throughout the evening, Rogers repeatedly referred to his opponent's promises as a "con."

Foreign Policy and Immigration Fronts

Foreign affairs sparked additional friction. Asked about tensions involving Israel and Iran, El-Sayed declined to single out one nation as a greater primary threat, stating that the U.S. should avoid being drawn deeper into Middle Eastern military commitments and instead focus federal resources on domestic education, healthcare, and infrastructure.

On immigration, Rogers sought to highlight El-Sayed’s past calls to abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). When questioned about past aggressive enforcement tactics under the Trump administration, Rogers offered a nuanced critique of a high-profile Minneapolis operation, drawing on his background as a federal agent to argue for quieter, tactical law enforcement strategies rather than public spectacles.

Personal Jabs and High Campaign Stakes

Beyond policy debates, the candidates frequently engaged in personal attacks, targeting each other over property holdings in Florida and the United Arab Emirates, as well as trading petty personal insults. The race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters remains one of the most closely watched Senate battles in the nation, with partisan control of the chamber potentially hinging on Michigan's outcome.

Addressing recent rhetoric from national Republicans targeting his faith and background, El-Sayed brushed off personal attacks during a campaign stop earlier in the day, insisting voters care far more about pocketbook issues than political slurs. The candidates are scheduled to meet once more before Election Day.
